newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Stability decays in Nicaragua before anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Stability decays in Nicaragua before anniversary.

text.p: Nicaragua, tense after weeks of clashes between protesters and police, is growing increasingly unstable because of a conflict between the government and the Sandinista opposition, political analysts said on Friday.
Pitched battles between police and students over the last three weeks have left 150 people injured.

Fears that the country -- still polarised between the left-wing Sandinista Front and right-wing rulers -- could slide back into the open conflict that plagued the country from 1979-1990 have set citizens' nerves on edge.
On Wednesday hundreds of Nicaraguans took to the streets waving white handkerchiefs for peace.
But analysts blamed the eroding stability on intransigence between the governing Alianza Liberal and the opposition Sandinista Front (FSLN) since its defeat in November 1996.

"We have two big groups struggling to dominate each other," said Raul Obregon, director of independent national consultants M&R. "This struggle of the titans ... is causing a deterioration in stability."

Tensions are high in the run-up to Saturday's anniversary of the 1979 Sandinista revolution, and the recent strife has rattled Nicaraguans whose country has been riven by civil war for much of its modern history.

There are widespread fears the Sandinistas are planning disruptions in the northern city of Esteli -- the scene of bitter fighting during the Sandinista's war against U.S.-backed Contras in the 1980s.
Francois Houtart, at the Centre for Sociocultural Analysis, pointed to the government for much of the trouble.
"The FSLN has the will to sign an agreement which will allow it to survive, but the government does not want to cede," he said.
Obregon said work for reconciliation under Nicaragua's former President Violeta Chamorro was being betrayed.
"All that was achieved in those years to reinforce an attitude of conciliation and to foster a common national project for all Nicaraguans is falling apart," he said.

Chamorro was elected president in 1990 after eight years of civil war. She risked her popularity by extending a conciliatory hand to the Sandinistas in a pact that laid down the basis for coexistence between victors and vanquished.
But her successor Arnoldo Aleman, of the governing alliance, insisted he would never make a pact with the Sandinistas after he came to power in November 1996.

Aleman has tried to ease tension by calling leaders from all Nicaragua's political, labour and professional groups to participate in a "national dialogue" next week, but the Sandinistas say they will not take part.
